aliases: Y single atoms on N-doped carbon

nodes.name: Host-guest encapsulation
nodes.procedure: The Y(acac)3@ZIF-8 precursor was initially fabricated following the reported host–guest strategy. During this process, Zn-based zeolitic imidazolate framework (ZIF-8) nanocrystals were employed as hosts to trap yttrium acetylacetonate (Y(acac)3) guest molecules.
nodes.source_text: The synthetic route for the Ru–YNC is depicted in Fig. 1(a). Briefly, the Y(acac)3@ZIF-8 precursor was initially fabricated following the reported host–guest strategy.

nodes.name: Pyrolysis and acid etching
nodes.procedure: Subsequently, the Y(acac)3@ZIF-8 precursor underwent the pyrolysis and acid etching treatment to prepare the YNC, which was constituted of isolated Y SAs immobilized on a N-doped carbon support. The Zn atoms in the Y(acac)3@ZIF-8 precursor were essentially evaporated during the pyrolysis process at 950 °C, and further completely removed by the subsequent acid etching treatment owing to the weak Zn–N coordination in acidic media.

nodes.source_text: Subsequently, the Y(acac)3@ZIF-8 precursor underwent the pyrolysis and acid etching treatment to prepare the YNC

nodes.name: Impregnation-reduction
nodes.procedure: The Ru–YNC that comprises ultrasmall Ru clusters anchored on the YNC support was ultimately synthesized via an impregnation-reduction method, which involved the adsorption of Ru3+ ions and annealing under a reducing atmosphere.
nodes.source_text: The Ru–YNC that comprises ultrasmall Ru clusters anchored on the YNC support was ultimately synthesized via an impregnation-reduction method

nodes.name: ZIF-8 pyrolysis
nodes.procedure: For comparison, the Ru–NC without Y SAs was also prepared through the similar procedure except for employing the N-doped carbon support directly pyrolyzed from the ZIF-8 precursor.
nodes.source_text: the N-doped carbon support directly pyrolyzed from the ZIF-8 precursor

nodes.description: Alkaline HER LSV performance in 1.0 M KOH three-electrode system
nodes.source_text: The electrochemical alkaline HER performance of the Ru–YNC was evaluated in N₂-saturated 1.0 M KOH solution using a standard three-electrode system... LSV curves with 95% iR-correction exhibit extremely low overpotentials of 22 and 109 mV at current densities of 10 and 100 mA cm⁻²... Tafel slope of the Ru–YNC is only 39 mV dec⁻¹... noble metal mass activity of 17.79 A mg noble metal-1 at -0.1 V vs. RHE... TOF values... 7.9 s⁻¹ at -0.1 V vs. RHE

nodes.description: AEMWE steady-state polarization and stability at 80°C

nodes.characterization_summary: HAADF-STEM images of Ru–YNC exhibit numerous well-dispersed metal clusters with an average particle size of 2.2 nm.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The HAADF-STEM images of the Ru–YNC exhibit numerous well-dispersed metal clusters with an average particle size of only 2.2 nm (Fig. 1(b) and (c)).

nodes.characterization_summary: HRTEM images show lattice fringes with spacing of 0.214 nm assigned to the (002) plane of hcp Ru.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Furthermore, the high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images disclose that the individual metal cluster presents lattice fringes with a spacing of 0.214 nm (Fig. S9, ESI†), which can be assigned to the (002) plane of hexagonal close-packed (hcp) Ru.

properties.description: High-Resolution Transmission Electron Microscopy image labeled (e)

nodes.characterization_summary: AC-HAADF-STEM confirms coexistence of Ru clusters and Y single atoms; atomic arrangements match (002) plane of hcp Ru.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Notably, the coexistence of Ru clusters and Y SAs (encircled by red circles) is distinctly visualized in the AC-HAADF-STEM images of the Ru–YNC (Fig. 1(f) and Fig. S11, ESI†).

nodes.characterization_summary: EDX elemental mapping shows Ru concentrated on clusters, Y evenly distributed on N-doped carbon support.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Meanwhile, the elemental distribution is revealed using the AC-HAADF-STEM energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) elemental mapping analysis. As shown in Fig. 1(g), the Ru signal is mainly concentrated on monodispersed metal clusters, while the Y signal is evenly distributed throughout the N-doped carbon support.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru content 0.95 wt% and Y content 0.91 wt% in Ru–YNC.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The specific contents of Ru and Y elements in the Ru–YNC were determined to be 0.95 and 0.91 wt.%, respectively, by inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectrometry (ICP-AES) (Table S1, ESI†).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru–YNC shows no Ru diffraction peaks due to ultrasmall cluster size; Ru–NC shows slight peak at 44° for hcp Ru (101).
nodes.evidence_snippet: Remarkably, no XRD diffraction peaks ascribed to the hcp Ru are detected in the Ru–YNC due to the ultrasmall size of the monodispersed Ru clusters. In contrast, the Ru–NC containing Ru clusters with an average size of 3.1 nm exhibits a slight XRD peak at approximately 44° corresponding to the (101) plane of the hcp Ru (Fig. 1(d) and Fig. S10, ESI†).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru–YNC Ru 3p peaks shifted -0.3 eV lower vs Ru–NC indicating electron-enriched Ru; increased Ru⁰ fraction; Y 3d shifted +0.4 eV vs YNC.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In comparison with the Ru–NC without Y SAs, the peak area of Ru⁴⁺ in the Ru–YNC exhibit a significant reduction, accompanied by an increase of Ru⁰... the peak positions of Ru 3p in the Ru–YNC shift towards lower binding energies relative to those of the Ru–NC with an approximate negative shift of about 0.3 eV... the high-resolution Y 3d spectrum of the Ru–YNC displays a positive shift of about 0.4 eV compared to that of the YNC.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru K-edge shows reduced oxidation state in Ru–YNC vs Ru–NC; Y K-edge shows positive shift in Ru–YNC vs YNC.
nodes.evidence_snippet: the Ru K-edge XANES spectra reveal that the edge energy of the Ru–YNC is close to that of the Ru foil (Ru⁰) and exhibits a negative shift relative to that of the Ru–NC... a slightly positive shift in the edge energy of the Ru–YNC compared with that of the YNC is observed in the Y K-edge XANES spectra (Fig. 2(c) and (d)).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru K-edge: Ru–Ru at 2.48 Å (CN=5.7 in Ru–YNC vs 6.8 in Ru–NC), Ru–N at 1.58 Å (CN=1.5); Y K-edge: Y–N at 1.71 Å (CN≈4), no Y–Y or Y–O confirming atomic dispersion.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The corresponding EXAFS quantitative fitting results confirm that the average coordination numbers of Ru–Ru and Ru–N bonds in the Ru–YNC are 5.7 and 1.5, respectively... It is evident that the coordination number of Ru–Ru in the Ru–YNC has decreased relative to that in the Ru–NC without Y SAs (6.8)... the average coordination number of Y–N bond approaches 4.

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru–YNC ID/IG ratio = 1.03 indicating increased carbon defects from metal anchoring.
nodes.evidence_snippet: the corresponding ID/IG intensity ratios of the Ru–YNC (1.03) and YNC (1.02) are slightly higher than that of the pristine NC (1.01) (Fig. S13, ESI†)

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru–YNC specific surface area 623.5 m²/g; Ru–NC 511.6 m²/g.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Evidently, the Ru–YNC demonstrates a considerably larger specific surface area (623.5 m² g⁻¹) in comparison with the Ru–NC (511.6 m² g⁻¹).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ru–YNC and Ru–NC maintain rhombododecahedral morphology with diameter 300-400 nm.
nodes.evidence_snippet: It can be observed that both the Ru–YNC and Ru–NC still maintain the rhombododecahedral morphology with a diameter ranging from 300 to 400 nm (Fig. S7 and S8, ESI†).

nodes.characterization_summary: YNC magnified TEM shows no bulk nanoparticles; SAED confirms absence of crystalline Y phases.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Moreover, no noticeable bulk nanoparticles or clusters are observed in the magnified TEM image and corresponding selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern (Fig. S4d, ESI†).
